Read the package documentation

One chat for every bitbaum product. A composer with a microphone that never goes dead, a thread that does not fight the reader, answers with Copy and Retry, and LLM markdown — the fleet's chat standard as a package, so a fix made once reaches every product.

Why it exists: on 2026-09-25 there were 13 chats in 10 repos, each written from scratch, each missing something another had already fixed — most often the microphone. The person using them found every gap by hand. This package is the one place those fixes now live. (Model calls, streaming and transcription stay in ai-kit, server-side; chatkit is the interface that calls them.)

Install

pnpm add @bitbaum/chatkit

Install releases from npm, never a commit or a branch. A semver range is what lets a fix reach every product: Renovate/Dependabot opens the bump PR in each app when a release ships. A pinned commit or tag silently freezes the app on whatever it pinned — heidi and substrata kept the broken Android paperclip for days after the fix merged, because one pinned v0.2.0 and npm had only 0.2.1.

Use

import { ChatStarters, ChatThread, Composer } from "@bitbaum/chatkit/react";
import "@bitbaum/chatkit/styles.css";

<ChatThread
  messages={messages}               // { id, role, content, speaker?, citations?, failed? }
  live={streaming ? { text: partial } : null}
  onStop={stop}
  onRetry={retryLast}
  empty={<ChatStarters starters={["What can you build for me?"]} onPick={send} />}
/>
<Composer
  onSend={(text, attachments) => send(text, attachments)} // return false to keep the draft
  placeholder="Ask about any project…"
  sending={streaming}
  onStop={stop}
  voice={{ transcribeUrl: "/api/transcribe" }}
  attach                             // only if your API accepts attachments
  tools={<ModelPicker />}            // app-specific controls go in slots
  heldAttachments={refs.length}      // attachments the APP keeps (shown in `header`)
  attachmentOnlyText="See attached"  //   so a message of only those can still send
/>

The whole screen — ChatScreen

A chat page is the conversation, edge to edge and top to bottom, as in the ChatGPT and Claude apps. The header and the composer float OVER it instead of each taking a strip of the screen: words scroll under both and fade as they pass, the header's buttons are frosted pills (ck-glass), and the composer is a see-through pill. The last line of an answer always rests above the composer — the scroller is padded by the measured height of each.

<ChatScreen
  fill="viewport"                    // or "parent": fill the box you give it
  header={<>
    <button className="ck-glass" aria-label="Chats"><IconMenu /></button>
    <span style={{ flex: 1 }} />
    <button className="ck-glass" aria-label="New chat"><IconPen /></button>
  </>}
  composer={<Composer … />}           // plus an error or a queue, if you have one
  footnote="Answers can be wrong."
>
  <ChatThread … />
</ChatScreen>

fill="viewport" follows the VISUAL viewport, so the composer rides above the phone keyboard. An app with its own thread pads its scroller with the two measured heights: padding-block: var(--ck-top-inset) var(--ck-bottom-inset). The reading column is --ck-measure (48rem) wide with --ck-gutter (1rem) to the edge; the page behind it is --ck-page. demo/screen.html is the reference: look at it at 390px before changing any of this.

The whole app — ChatApp

ChatScreen, Composer and ChatThread are the pieces. Until 0.18 every product built the app around them itself — the chat list, New chat, Temporary chat, titles, rename and delete, what a reload reopens — and each did it a little differently (docs/fleet-chat-matrix.md has the table). ChatApp is that app, once: what a person sees in the Claude or ChatGPT phone app, set by this package and changed only through props.

import { ChatApp } from "@bitbaum/chatkit/react";
import { httpConversationStore, localConversationStore } from "@bitbaum/chatkit";

const store = signedIn
  ? httpConversationStore({ baseUrl: "/api/conversations" })
  : localConversationStore({ key: "heidi-chat" });

<ChatApp
  name="Heidi"
  store={store}
  transport={async ({ text, attachments, history, signal, update }) => {
    const answer = await streamFromMyApi({ text, attachments, history, signal, onText: (t) => update({ text: t }) });
    return answer; // a string, or { content, replies?, citations?, thinking? }
  }}
  composer={{ voice: { transcribeUrl: "/api/transcribe" } }}
  starters={["Explain this word", "Translate a message"]}
/>;

What it owns, so no product writes it again:

  • The header: frosted pills — Chats (a phone; from railQuery, default

64rem, the list is a rail beside the chat instead) · the chat's title · New chat · "…" with Temporary chat, Share this chat (with onShare), Rename and Delete. headerStart / headerEnd take the product's own controls (a model picker, a back link).

  • The chat list: a full-height drawer on a phone (a native <dialog>:

Escape, the focus trap and focus restore come from the browser; it opens on its close button, never on the search box, so no keyboard jumps up), a rail on a wide screen. New chat, a search box (every word, accents ignored — or your search, e.g. searchkit), Today / Yesterday / Earlier, and rows with ONE anatomy: title, date (or "Answering…"), one "…" that opens Rename · Delete as two equal cells; Delete asks once, in the row. An empty list and a failed load each say so, the second with Try again.

  • New chat and Temporary chat. A temporary chat is never written to the

store and ends when it is left; the transport gets temporary: true and conversationId: null, so a server that persists turns itself knows not to.

  • Titles: the first message names a chat (deriveTitle, Heidi's rule);

makeTitle({ text, answer }) renames it after the first answer if you have something better.

  • Reload: the open chat comes back (rememberKey, device storage — never

a temporary one), unless it was deleted elsewhere. A product that keeps the chat in its URL passes conversationId and onConversationChange instead.

  • Turns: one per conversation, and a turn keeps running when the person

opens another chat (its row says "Answering…"). Stop keeps what had arrived. A failed turn shows Retry. A message sent while an answer runs is queued above the composer, with its own ×, and goes when the answer lands.

  • The composer: attachments ON (Camera · Photos · Files, thumbnails above

the text, each with its ×, shown in the sent turn too), the microphone, suggested replies, and the screen's visual-viewport sizing (fill).

The transport is the product's one job: (turn) => Promise<answer>. turn is { conversationId, temporary, text, attachments, history, signal, update }; call update({ text, status, steps }) as the answer streams (the whole text each time); throw for a failed turn.

The store is an adapter — six methods, ConversationStore: list() · get(id) · create({ title }) · append(id, message) · rename(id, title) · remove(id). Two come with the package:

  • localConversationStore({ key }) — the device. Versioned (<key>:v1),

one key per chat; never throws: storage that is missing, blocked (private mode) or full degrades to memory for the page, and a full quota drops the OLDEST chats first. Pictures are kept by name, not bytes.

  • httpConversationStore({ baseUrl }) — the product's server, over

Heidi's shape: GET {base} → { conversations }, POST {base} → { conversation }, GET {base}/{id} → { conversation, messages } (404 = gone), POST {base}/{id}/messages { message }, PATCH {base}/{id} { title }, DELETE {base}/{id}. serverWritesTurns: true when the product's chat route already stores each turn, so nothing is written twice.

Signed out on the device, signed in on the server: pass the store for who is there. copyConversations(local, server) moves the device's chats into the account on sign-in.

demo/app.html is the reference — look at it at 390px and 1440px. test/browser-app.mjs drives it at both widths: send, the drawer (focus in and back out), New chat, a temporary chat that leaves no row, a reload that reopens the chat, a picture staged above the text and removed, delete, the queue and Stop — and checks for sideways scroll, 44px targets and cut words at every step.

Moving a product onto ChatApp

Per product, from the matrix: what goes, what stays. What stays is always the same two things — the transport and the words.

  • Loki — goes: ThreadRail.tsx, the history half of

WorkspaceDrawers.tsx and WorkspaceChrome.tsx, ThreadTitle.tsx, hooks/use-temporary-chat.ts, hooks/use-new-chat.ts, hooks/use-send-queue.ts + QueuedMessages.tsx, the history-pin storage. Stays: use-loki-stream as the transport (its ephemeral flag from turn.temporary), ModelPicker and the project chip in composer.tools, the dispatch and handoff cards in thread.renderFooter, httpConversationStore({ baseUrl: "/api/conversations", serverWritesTurns: true }), ?c= through conversationId. Not in ChatApp yet, so ask for it here first: pinned chats, the "needs me first" line and by-project view, hands-free voice conversation.

  • OrangeCat — goes: ConversationRail.tsx, hooks/useConversations.ts

(incl. its temporary chat), hooks/useChatHistory.ts, the header row of ChatHeader.tsx. Stays: the Cat's stream as the transport, ComposerAddMenu (the person's own things) in composer.tools with heldAttachments, tool chips and pending actions in thread.renderFooter, the quota meter in headerEnd. Its conversation routes are not the REST shape above: a six-method store over API_ROUTES.CAT, or align the routes. Gains: reopening the chat after a reload, rename, search.

  • Heidi — goes: conversation-list.tsx, new-chat-button.tsx, the

header and drawer state in workspace.tsx, the storage half of use-conversation.ts, the signed-out draft restore (use-draft) → localConversationStore. Stays: transports.ts (its Transport maps onto this one: onText → update, a status: "error" result → a throw), the composer labels and picture limits, the answer view and word pick in thread.renderFooter, the model sheet in headerEnd. Store: httpConversationStore({ baseUrl: "/api/conversations", serverWritesTurns: true }) signed in. Gains: a temporary chat.

  • Substrata — goes: the ChatScreen + Composer + ChatThread

assembly in ResearchChat.tsx, lib/ask-thread.ts (the tab handoff → conversationId + the device store). Stays: useChatSession as the transport, AskTools / ComposerBeside in composer.tools and footnote, chartRenderers, AnswerFooter. Decide: attachments are ON in ChatApp; /api/chat takes no files today, so either keep composer={{ attach: false }} or accept pictures there.

  • Diplodoctor — goes: the assembly in app/[locale]/ask/page.tsx.

Stays: the redacting ask() as the transport, the labels. Gains: a chat list and reload. Needs: a transcription route (voice is off today) and an API that takes files before attach is turned on.

  • Causius — stays as it is for now. A matter is a case with documents,

participants and steps, not a chat; its list is the matters page. ChatThread + IntakeComposer remain the right pieces.

  • evig — goes: the header and Clear in HirnChat.tsx and

HirnChatPanel.tsx. Stays: /api/hirn/chat as the transport, the action cards in thread.renderFooter, useChatLabels. Store: the Hirn history route is per session, not the REST shape — a six-method store, or the device store for the panel.

  • Solon — goes: the header, "New conversation" and the React-state

history in governance-chat.tsx and law-chat.tsx. Stays: the SSE read as the transport, the starters, renderLink. Gains: chats that survive a reload (the footnote promises "stays in this tab" and today nothing does). Signed out keeps its own "Sign in to ask Solon" screen instead of ChatApp.

The microphone

voice is on by default. Give it a server leg so it works everywhere:

  • transcribeUrl: an endpoint taking multipart/form-data { audio, locale }

and answering { text } — implement it with ai-kit's transcribe().

  • or transcribe: (audio, locale) => Promise<string> for a custom call.

The browser's own recogniser is tried first (free, instant). Where it is missing, or accepts start() and then says nothing — Chromium without Google's speech service does exactly that — the same press records and the server transcribes. The dead recogniser is remembered for 30 days so the next press records immediately. Every failure is shown in words (blocked mic, nothing heard, not available), never as a button that does nothing. prefer: "server" skips the browser leg (one model everywhere, language detected by the model). rememberKey: null stores nothing on the device.

Suggested replies

The two to four things the person is likely to say next, as buttons under the latest answer — one tap sends it. The model writes them in the same turn, so there is no second call and no wait:

import { REPLIES_INSTRUCTION } from "@bitbaum/chatkit";
const system = `${yourPrompt}\n\n${REPLIES_INSTRUCTION}`; // server side
<ChatThread messages={messages} onReply={send} … />

Below 40rem the replies are one row that scrolls sideways with a fade, the lead reply first and always on screen; wider, they wrap. The Copy · Listen · Share · Retry row under an answer keeps each word on one line and every button at the 44px target (0.12.1).

That is the whole integration. ChatThread takes the quick_replies block out of every answer (and out of a streaming one before it has finished, so nobody watches JSON appear), and shows the buttons under the latest answer only, never while a turn runs. Pass replies on a message to supply your own instead. An app with its own thread uses extractReplies(text) and <ChatReplies>, so the buttons look and behave the same everywhere.

The model leads. The instruction asks for replies on EVERY answer, the recommended next step first, and the first button is drawn as the lead (ck-reply-lead): on a phone the answer is read and the next move is one tap, the way Grok does it. Only an answer that ends the conversation has no buttons.

No heading over the buttons (0.15.1). Models like to write their own "Quick follow-up options" (or "Suggested replies", "Mögliche Rückfragen:", …) as the last line above the block; drawn over the buttons it reads as an empty section. The instruction tells the model not to, and extractReplies drops it anyway — decided by shape and position, not a word list, so it holds in every language: the last block before the replies, a heading or a bold/italic-only line of at most six words with no sentence punctuation but a closing colon, plus an --- beside it. A bold sentence ("China holds 99 %.") stays. While streaming ({ streaming: true }, which ChatThread passes) such a line is held back until the next line shows what it is, so it never flashes. dropReplyLabel(text) is exported for apps that pass their own replies.

Under every answer — Copy, Listen, Share

AnswerActions is the row under an answer, the same in every product:

<AnswerActions text={answer} onRetry={retry} speaker={studioVoice} share={{ url }}>
  <YourOwnButton />
</AnswerActions>

Copy copies the markdown. Listen reads the answer aloud as prose (headings, emphasis, citations and code fences stripped — plainTextForSpeech) with the browser's own voice, or with the speaker you pass ({ speak(text), cancel() } — loki hands in its studio voice); while it reads, the row becomes a small player: Stop and the time so far. Share opens the system share sheet with the answer's prose (or what you pass), only where one exists. A button that does nothing is never shown. ChatThread renders it under every answer; pass speaker and share through.

Dictation reads Android's cumulative results once (0.15.2)

Android's Chrome-family recognisers (Chrome, Brave, Samsung Internet) report one utterance cumulatively — "why", "why exactly", "why exactly is", … — often every one of them flagged final. The hook appended every final, so Substrata's Ask box on Brave typed the sentence once per word (2026-10-25). The transcript is now rebuilt from the recogniser's whole results list on every event by heardFromResults (core, pure), which collapses a growing chain to its last link. Desktop finals are untouched: two different phrases stay two, and a word the person really repeats as separate results stays repeated. The one limitation — "no" then "no no" as two separate results reads as one utterance growing — is written down beside the rule. test/dictation.test.js holds the fixtures; test/browser.mjs drives the real composer with a fake cumulative recogniser and fails on the old hook.

Charts in answers (0.15)

"Who produces gallium?" is answered with a ranked bar chart, not a list. chatkit stays dependency-free: it defines the data contract and a renderer slot; the drawing is the app's. Substrata injects @bitbaum/chartkit, whose components take exactly the block's fields, so a block spreads into the matching one:

import { BarChart, LineChart, ShareBars, Timeline, StatTiles } from "@bitbaum/chartkit";
const renderers = {
  chart: (b) =>
    b.chart === "bars" ? <BarChart {...b} /> : b.chart === "line" ? <LineChart {...b} /> : b.chart === "share" ? <ShareBars {...b} /> : b.chart === "timeline" ? <Timeline {...b} /> : <StatTiles {...b} />,
};
<ChatScreen renderers={renderers} …>   // every answer on the screen
<ChatThread renderers={renderers} …>   // or one thread; Markdown and RichAnswerBlock take it too

Without a renderer, or when one returns null for a kind it does not draw, chatkit draws the fallback itself: the caption and a .ck-table of the data, so a chart is never a blank. A malformed block (a share of 140, a link with a script in it) is rejected by the parser and degrades to the same table of whatever rows were safe — the renderer never sees it. Copy and Listen read the figures as lines.

The model writes a chart in the same fenced chat_ui JSON as every other block. RICH_ANSWERS_INSTRUCTION now says when to draw one — ranked quantities with 3+ rows → bars; shares of one whole → share; a quantity over time with 3+ points → line; 3+ dated events → timeline; 2–4 headline figures → tiles — that every number comes from a tool result, and that each row's href is copied from the result's page or link.

The contract (ChartBlock, exported; limits are the parser's):

{ type: "chart", chart: "bars",     caption, unit?, highlight?, rows: [{ label, value, href?, share?, note?, estimated? }] }   // ≤ 24 rows
{ type: "chart", chart: "share",    caption, other?, rows: [{ label, share, href? }] }                                        // share 0–100
{ type: "chart", chart: "line",     caption, unit?, series: [{ id, label, points: [{ x, y, href?, note? }] }] }               // ≤ 6 series, ≤ 120 points
{ type: "chart", chart: "timeline", caption, events: [{ date, label, href?, tone?: "up" | "down" | "neutral", kind? }] }     // ≤ 24 events
{ type: "chart", chart: "tiles",    caption, tiles: [{ label, value, href?, note? }] }                                       // ≤ 6 tiles

An href is a same-site path or a web URL, never anything else. The block sits in the answer column with the stack figure's margins (.ck-rich .ck-chart); test/browser.mjs renders one through a stub renderer and one through the fallback at 320, 390 and 1280px, runs the broken-word scan over them and asserts no horizontal overflow.

Words are never cut (0.14.1)

A word may wrap onto the next line; it may never be cut in two. .ck-md sets overflow-wrap: anywhere so a long URL cannot push the thread wider, but anywhere also lowers a table cell's minimum width to one letter, and Substrata's three-column answer at 390px read "Te / rm" and "Di / re / ct / or / y" (2026-10-22). Tables now keep every word whole: columns share the width by wrapping at spaces, and when even the words do not fit the table scrolls sideways with a shadow on the edge that has more. The stack figure's tiles wrap too: three across becomes two and one, or one under the other, rather than cut "Manufacture".

test/browser.mjs measures it rather than reading the CSS: every word on the page is laid out in a Range at 320, 390 and 1280px and must sit on one line (a word beside a hyphen, slash or dot, and anything over 24 characters, is exempt: a URL has to break somewhere). The demo thread carries the table from the screenshot, so the check fails on the old stylesheet.

The check is exported so any product can run it against its own pages, from a Playwright script (never from app code):

import { BROKEN_WORDS_SOURCE } from "@bitbaum/chatkit/audit";
const broken = await page.evaluate(`(${BROKEN_WORDS_SOURCE})(document.body)`);
if (broken.length) throw new Error(`words cut across lines: ${broken}`);

The feedback loop (0.14)

Two halves, one shape, so a bad answer is found by the product, not by the owner tripping over it.

  • Under every answer, a thumb up and a thumb down — pass onFeedback to

ChatThread (or messageId + onFeedback to AnswerActions). A thumb down opens a sheet: one tap on why (FEEDBACK_REASONS: wrong, gave up instead of looking, vague, misread, too long, hard to read, other), words optional, then Send. The app gets { messageId, verdict, reason?, text? } and keeps it with the conversation.

  • A nightly judge. A product exports a day of conversations as

ChatTranscript[] (turns with the steps the assistant took, plus the thumbs); a reviewer asks a model, with CHAT_REVIEW_INSTRUCTION and reviewPrompt(scope, transcript), what the person most likely wanted, what the product could have given with the tools it has, and what it gave, and reads the verdicts back with parseChatReview (score 1–5, gaps from REVIEW_GAPS: dead_end, wrong_tool, no_web, misread, vague, no_next_step…, and one concrete fix). In the fleet, Loki runs the judge and files each gap into its feedback inbox, where fixes are built.

The next message while a turn runs

queue keeps Send live while sending, beside Stop, and the placeholder reads "Queue a message…": the app receives the message through onSend as usual and sends it on when the turn ends. Without it a send during a turn is refused, which holds the next thought until a spinner stops.

Recordings

With a server leg, the paperclip also takes a recording that already exists — a voice memo from the phone's recorder, a taped meeting. It is dictation that happened earlier: the file is posted to transcribeUrl under its own name (Whisper reads the container from the extension) and the words land in the box like a mic take, never staged as an attachment the model would have to read. Files are recognised by type and, where a picker hands them over typeless as Android does with .m4a, by extension. Uploads are capped at MAX_AUDIO_FILE_BYTES (120 MB — an hour of phone memo with room to spare); over it, the person is told in words before any bytes move. Your server leg should compress and split long audio before Whisper; loki's does.

Camera, Photos, Files

On a touch screen the paperclip opens a sheet with three choices — Camera, Photos, Files — each its own file input. One input with a mixed accept (image/*,text/*,audio/*) is what a phone answers with a chooser of capture apps (Camera, Camera, Recorder, "Photos & Videos"), where the screenshot you came to send is three levels down and the file browser is not offered at all. ATTACH_SOURCE_INPUT is the SSOT: Camera captures, Photos opens the system photo picker, Files has no accept and opens the real document browser. Because Files takes anything, isTextFile decides afterwards what can be read inline; a PDF gets a sentence, not a prompt full of bytes. With a mouse the paperclip opens the file dialog directly — on a desktop all three are the same dialog. A box that is not chatkit's composer renders <AttachMenu onFiles={…} /> rather than a bare <input type="file">. An app with more to bring into a message than files — one of the person's own things, a note the model reads every time — passes extra={(close) => <YourRows />}: the rows sit under the three sources in the same sheet, and the sheet then opens on a mouse too, since a file dialog cannot hold them. Labels: labels={{ attachMenu: { title, close, sources: { camera, photos, files } } }}.

Picking files anywhere — @bitbaum/chatkit/attach

An app with no chat still has uploaders (an avatar, product photos, a receipt). They need the same thing from a phone, so they use the same piece:

import { AttachMenu, shrinkImage } from "@bitbaum/chatkit/attach";

<AttachMenu
  sources={["camera", "photos"]} // an image uploader offers no Files
  trigger="Add photo"
  onFiles={(files) => upload(files)}
/>;

sources narrows the sheet (one source skips it). shrinkImage(file, maxEdge, maxBytes) is the in-browser downscale the composer uses. acceptFamilies and ATTACH_SOURCE_INPUT are the rule itself.

The check every app runs in CI

pnpm exec chatkit-check-file-inputs            # src app components

Fails on any file input whose literal accept mixes families (image + text, audio + text…) — the exact shape that hid screenshots on Android. One input per family, or AttachMenu. A real exception carries // chatkit-allow-mixed-accept: <reason> on the line or the line above.

Screenshots

attach takes limits: attach={{ maxImageEdge: 1024 }} shrinks a picture in the browser to 1024px on its longest edge and re-encodes it as JPEG before it is staged, stepping quality down until it fits maxImageBytes. A phone screenshot (~1290×2796, several MB) goes out at a few hundred KB: cheaper for whoever pays for the vision model, and the full-resolution screenshot never leaves the device. Off by default (0).

Every reason a file did not attach is a label — labels={{ attachNotes: { imageTooLarge: (name, mb) => … } }} — so it reaches the reader in their language.

The look of an answer

Markdown renders what a model writes, never as HTML: paragraphs, headings with their level, bullet, numbered, nested and task lists, tables (they scroll sideways on a phone instead of breaking the page), rules, bold, italic, code, links, web images and [F1] citation handles. Three things make an answer read like the ChatGPT app's rather than a wall of text, and a model does all three unprompted:

  • A list of named things becomes cards. 1. **Option.** why — every item

opening with a bold lead — renders as a badge (the number, or the emoji the lead opens with: **🤖 Robot.** …), the name, and the body under it.

  • A table is a table, with the header row kept.
  • Sources are listed once, under the answer, from the handles the text

cites and the citations map you pass ({ F1: { label, detail, href? } }). On a mouse they are a row of chips; on a touch screen ONE "Sources · n" button opens a sheet with every record — label, detail, link — because a row of chips on a phone was a row of cut-off words. renderCitation replaces the in-text superscript with your own; renderSources replaces the row with your own; sources={false} drops it. SourcesRow and Sheet are exported for an app that lists sources from elsewhere.

0.13 — answers that read like the ChatGPT app's, measured against it screen by screen on a phone:

  • Headings are signposts: a size up, with air above them, so a long

answer can be scanned and found again.

  • Options are cards: a numbered list whose items open with a bold name

gets a tile badge, the name a size up, a hairline between cards, and a pill for a short tag written right after the name — 1. **Federated.** [Recommended] …. The instruction asks the model to mark the one it recommends exactly that way.

  • Sources are chips: a [F2, F1] handle is drawn after the sentence as

"Fleet AGENTS.md +1", linked when the record has a link, and moved after the full stop when the model wrote it before. renderCitation still replaces it.

  • Links that leave the site say so: a dotted underline and a small arrow.
  • A layered figure — {"type":"stack", …} — for an architecture, a

pipeline or layers of responsibility: full-width boxes top to bottom, a row of tiles where a layer has parts (with an icon from a closed list), the words that cross each arrow, an accent tone for the layer that matters, and a caption that says what the figure claims. diagram stays for an arbitrary graph.

  • "Thought for 3m 38s ›" above an answer, from message.thinking

({ durationMs?, steps?: [{ label, detail? }], summary? }), closed by default; while a turn runs, live.steps shows the same row open with the newest step marked. ThinkingRow is exported for an app's own thread.

demo/screen.html shows all of it.

Look

Every colour, radius and face is a --ck-* variable. They default to @bitbaum/design-tokens, so OrangeCat, Loki, Solon and bitbaum match with no work. Any other app sets --ck-* on the chat's container and keeps its own look. What you cannot change is the behaviour — that is the point.

Language

Every visible word is a label: labels={{ send: "Senden", dictation: {...} }} on Composer, labels on ChatThread.

The standard (what this package guarantees)

  1. A microphone in the composer, with the server fallback above — and the

same server leg for a recording picked as a file.

  1. 16px text in the input and the messages (below that iOS zooms the page).
  2. A composer that belongs to the conversation: auto-growing textarea, Enter

sends, Shift+Enter breaks the line, IME composition respected, 44px targets, usable above the phone keyboard (useViewportHeight).

  1. Stop in the send slot while a turn is in flight.
  2. A failed turn shows as a failure with Retry — never silence.
  3. Scroll follows new tokens only while the reader is at the bottom, with a

jump-down button otherwise.

  1. Markdown rendered, never as HTML; javascript: links stay text; Copy on

every answer.

  1. Starters in the empty state; suggested replies under the latest answer;

the speaker's name on every answer once more than one agent speaks.

  1. Nothing overflows at 320–390px.
  2. In ChatScreen, the conversation fills the display and opens at the

latest message, with its end above the composer, not behind it.

  1. In ChatApp, the same app everywhere: one chat list with one row

anatomy, New chat, Temporary chat that writes nothing, the open chat back after a reload, attachments on, a queue behind a running answer.

pnpm run verify proves all of it: unit and render tests, then test/browser.mjs drives Chromium through the demo at desktop and 390px, light and dark, and speaks into a fake microphone past a silent recogniser.

Improving it — here, never in your app

When a chat in any product has a bug or is missing something, fix it in this repo, add the check that would have caught it, bump the version, and let the products pick the release up. A local patch in one app is how the fleet got 13 different chats. If your app needs something truly its own, it goes in a slot (tools, header, footer, renderFooter, renderLink) — ask for a new slot here rather than forking the component.

Release: bump version in package.json and merge. The merge publishes it (publish.yml runs on main, skips a version already on npm, and tags the commit v<version>). No manual tag.

Develop

pnpm install
pnpm run demo        # builds demo/dist; open demo/index.html
pnpm run verify      # everything CI runs

MIT © Cato

Visual answers (0.11)

Append RICH_ANSWERS_INSTRUCTION from @bitbaum/chatkit to a conversational system prompt, alongside REPLIES_INSTRUCTION. The model can place fenced chat_ui JSON blocks inline in its answer: galleries with captions and a full-size image sheet, dependency diagrams, recommendation callouts, and single-choice follow-ups. Markdown tables and step lists remain available. Markdown renders these automatically; pass onReply={send} for choice forms. ChatThread wires that callback only on the latest answer and disables it while another turn is running. Historical forms remain readable.

Products keep their own model routing, tools, evidence rules, auth and --ck-* tokens. For a JSON-output assistant such as Heidi, ask for rich blocks only inside its free-text explanation string, never outside the answer envelope. Images must come from supplied context or tool results. No HTML or executable SVG is accepted. Images suppress referrers and broken thumbnails retain their text labels. Blocks are bounded and validated; incomplete/invalid blocks are hidden, so always include the takeaway in ordinary prose too. Diagram edges retain their direction and labels, including branches and cycles.

Release this package before updating consumer lockfiles to ^0.11.0. Run pnpm run verify; demo/index.html is the visual reference in light/dark and at phone width. The diagram and gallery artwork in the demo is a fixture.

Audio in answers

A validated chat_ui block can attach a real audio asset:

{"type":"audio","title":"Morning sketch","src":"/provided.wav","creator":"Studio","caption":"An original instrumental draft"}

The native player waits for explicit playback and does not preload the file. Only attach URLs supplied by a person or a completed tool. Generation and catalogue access belong to the app's media tools: this renderer does not create a song or grant rights to redistribute it. Copy and speech preserve the track's title, creator and caption. The demo WAV is an original synthesized fixture; it is not a commercial track or a model-generated recording.

The browser word-layout audit uses Unicode word boundaries. Chinese, Japanese and Korean may wrap between characters; those legal breaks are accepted while squeezed Latin words, including words embedded in CJK text, are still reported. Whole-page and chart overflow checks remain separate.

Scrolling in a page or panel

ChatThread detects whether its own panel, an ancestor, or the page scrolls. Upward touch, wheel and keyboard gestures pause automatic following immediately, including close to the bottom. Status updates and incoming assistant turns keep the reading position. Sending a new user turn or choosing return-to-latest resumes following. Full-screen ChatScreen keeps its bounded scroll containment; embedded threads allow gestures to reach their surrounding page.
